newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire admits more war losses, still rejects talks.
newsitem.headline: Zaire admits more war losses, still rejects talks.

text.p: Zaire on Tuesday acknowleged more battlefield losses to guerrillas who have entered its Shaba mining province, but ruled out accepting rebel calls for talks.
Deputy foreign minister Henri-Thomas Lokondo Yoka told Reuters the government was concerned by recent rebel victories, including the seizure of the strategic Shaba port of Kalemie.
But he said there was no question of accepting the call by rebel leader Laurent Kabila for negotiations to end the Tutsi-led rebellion he launched last October.

"They may be winning battles but they have not won the war," Lokondo Yoka said. "Of course we are concerned but we are in the process of taking measures to retake all the occupied areas. You will see in the days to come."

The Zaire government ordered a massive mobilisation and turned to its African allies for help after rebels extended their campaign and territory they hold from the borders of Rwanda and Uganda to the mineral-rich Shaba Province.
A senior defence ministry official said Zaire was expecting troops from Togo, Chad and Morocco as well as material assistance from Egypt.
Togo denied planning to send troops. Egypt said it had no defence ties with Zaire. There was no word from Chad or Morocco, where Zaire's veteran ruler Mobutu Sese Sesko is visiting.

Zaire accuses neighbouring Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of sending their regular armies to back the rebels. Ethnic Tutsis originally took up arms after Zairean authorities threatened to uproot them to their ancestral homeland in Rwanda. Kabila now says he wants to end Mobutu's 31-year rule.
"We cannot negotiate with the rebels. They are, as you know, supported by certain countries," Lokonda Yoka said.
The army said on Tuesday that Rwandan-backed rebels had defeated Zaire soldiers at Kalemie.
A spokesman at army headquarters contradicted defence ministry officials who said only Kalemie port had fallen.
"The port is the town. We don't yet have the details but it is as you have heard. The town fell at 10 o'clock yesterday," the spokesman told Reuters.
He had no details of casualties or where Zairean troops based in the town were now headed.
Residents in the capital Kinshasa in contact with the port before it fell told Reuters hundreds of members of the local population fled the town by train three days earlier.
They said residents had begun fleeing the town of Kongolo, 250 km (150 miles) west of Kalemie in the same Shaba province, and also linked by rail to the provincial capital Lubumbashi.
Although some 800 km (500 miles) away from Shaba's copper and cobalt mines, Kalemie is a strategic commercial transit point with rail, air and lake connections to the entire region.

The state copper giant, Gecamines, is supplied with equipment and parts via the port at Kalemie, which is an important trading post between Zaire and neighbouring Tanzania, and further to Southern Africa through a rail link.
Kalemie also supplies by rail the neighbouring regions of Maniema and Kasai with agricultural and other produce, as well as serving as an export centre for the same areas.

The town is at the head of the Sizarail line that reaches all the way to South Africa. Its fall could be a big loss to the consortium of Belgian and South African companies that has dramatically improved the once crumbling railway.

The Zairean army is now fighting on at least three fronts as rebels spread their grip on the border regions both to the north and south, controlling now a strip of territory at least 1,000 km (600 miles) long.
